title: "Stimulant Dose × Outdoor Exposure: A 3×2 Factorial Experiment on 5 km Run Time"
author: "Jiho Kim"
output: github_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = "images/", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5,
                      dpi = 150, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
```

This notebook has two parts. **Part 1** reproduces the original course analysis
(UCLA STAT 101B, Design and Analysis of Experiments). **Part 2** re-validates it
the way an independent reviewer would: it checks whether the groups were
comparable, whether the model assumptions hold, which observations drive the
result, and whether the conclusions survive alternative methods.

# Part 1. Original analysis

## 1.1 Data

The data come from **The Islands**, a virtual population simulation used for
teaching experimental design. Each of 150 islanders ran 5 km before and after
a treatment. The two factors are:

- **Stimulant dose** (methamphetamine, as offered in the simulation): 0, 10 or 50
- **Outdoor exposure** (sitting outside): No (N) or Yes (Y)

The response is the **change in 5 km time** (after − before, in minutes).
A negative change means the islander ran faster.

```{r data}
data <- read.csv("data/islands_5km_experiment.csv")
data$change   <- data$after_5km - data$before_5km
data$dose     <- factor(data$Methamphetamine)
data$outdoors <- factor(data$Sitting_outside)

head(data)

# Balanced 3 x 2 design: 25 islanders in every cell
table(Dose = data$dose, Outdoors = data$outdoors)

# Mean change (minutes) in each cell
round(tapply(data$change, list(Dose = data$dose, Outdoors = data$outdoors), mean), 2)
```

## 1.2 Two-way ANOVA with interaction

```{r anova}
model <- aov(change ~ dose * outdoors, data = data)
summary(model)
```

No effect is significant at the 5% level. Outdoor exposure is borderline
(p ≈ 0.066), while stimulant dose and the interaction show no effect.

## 1.3 Visualization

```{r interaction_plot}
ggplot(data, aes(x = dose, y = change, group = outdoors,
                 color = outdoors, linetype = outdoors)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 2.5) +
  labs(title = "Interaction plot: mean change in 5 km time",
       x = "Stimulant dose", y = "Mean change in 5 km time (min)",
       color = "Sitting outside", linetype = "Sitting outside") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r boxplots, fig.height = 4}
p1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = dose, y = change, fill = dose)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "By stimulant dose", x = "Stimulant dose", y = "Change (min)") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

p2 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = outdoors, y = change, fill = outdoors)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "By outdoor exposure", x = "Sitting outside", y = "Change (min)") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none")

p3 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = dose, y = change, fill = outdoors)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Dose × outdoor exposure", x = "Stimulant dose",
       y = "Change (min)", fill = "Outdoors") +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3, widths = c(1, 1, 1.4))
```

# Part 2. Re-validation

## 2.1 Were the groups comparable at baseline?

If the treatment groups already differed before the treatment, any difference
afterwards could come from that imbalance rather than the treatment.

```{r baseline}
summary(aov(before_5km ~ dose * outdoors, data = data))   # baseline 5 km time
summary(aov(Age ~ dose * outdoors, data = data))          # age
chisq.test(table(data$Gender, interaction(data$dose, data$outdoors)))  # gender
```

Baseline run time and gender are balanced across cells. Age shows a small
imbalance in the interaction term (p ≈ 0.046), so age is added as a covariate
in the ANCOVA in section 2.6 to check whether it matters.

## 2.2 Are the ANOVA assumptions met?

```{r diagnostics, fig.height = 6}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)
```

```{r assumption_tests}
# Normality of residuals
shapiro.test(residuals(model))

# Equal variance: Bartlett (sensitive to non-normality)
bartlett.test(change ~ interaction(dose, outdoors), data = data)

# Equal variance: Brown-Forsythe (robust to non-normality)
brown_forsythe <- function(d) {
  cell   <- interaction(d$dose, d$outdoors)
  absdev <- abs(d$change - ave(d$change, cell, FUN = median))
  summary(aov(absdev ~ cell))[[1]][1, "Pr(>F)"]
}
brown_forsythe(data)
```

Normality fails badly (p < 0.001), and the Q-Q plot shows one point far above
the rest. Bartlett's test also rejects equal variance, but the robust
Brown-Forsythe test does not (p ≈ 0.09). This suggests the variance problem
is largely a side effect of the same non-normality.

## 2.3 Finding the outlier

```{r outlier}
fit <- lm(change ~ dose * outdoors, data = data)
std_res <- rstandard(fit)
cooks   <- cooks.distance(fit)
out_row <- which.max(std_res)

round(sort(std_res, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 2)   # top 3 standardized residuals
round(sort(cooks,   decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 3)   # top 3 Cook's distances

data[out_row, c("Name", "Age", "before_5km", "after_5km", "change",
                "dose", "outdoors")]
```

One islander ran 5 km **35.6 minutes slower** after treatment. Its
standardized residual (6.9) and Cook's distance (0.33) are both far larger
than the next observation (2.4 and 0.04), so it stands clearly apart.

The data give no reason to call this point an error, so it is **kept** in the
main results. The checks below ask a different question: would the
conclusions change without it?

## 2.4 Sensitivity analysis: refit without the outlier

```{r sensitivity}
data_wo  <- data[-out_row, ]
model_wo <- aov(change ~ dose * outdoors, data = data_wo)
summary(model_wo)

shapiro.test(residuals(model_wo))   # normality is restored
brown_forsythe(data_wo)             # equal variance still not rejected

p_with    <- summary(model)[[1]][1:3, "Pr(>F)"]
p_without <- summary(model_wo)[[1]][1:3, "Pr(>F)"]
data.frame(term = c("Dose", "Outdoors", "Dose:Outdoors"),
           p_with_outlier = round(p_with, 3),
           p_without_outlier = round(p_without, 3))
```

Removing a single observation restores normality and moves the outdoor effect
from p = 0.066 to p = 0.12. The only near-significant result was driven by
one islander.

```{r qq_comparison, fig.height = 4}
qq_plot <- function(m, title) {
  r <- data.frame(res = rstandard(lm(m)))
  ggplot(r, aes(sample = res)) +
    stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
    labs(title = title, x = "Theoretical quantiles",
         y = "Standardized residuals") +
    theme_minimal()
}
grid.arrange(qq_plot(model,    "With the outlier (Shapiro p < 0.001)"),
             qq_plot(model_wo, "Without the outlier (Shapiro p = 0.75)"),
             ncol = 2)
```

## 2.5 Rank-based tests: robust without deleting any data

Deleting data is not the only way to handle an outlier. Rank-based tests use
the order of the values instead of the values themselves, so one extreme
point has limited influence.

```{r rank_tests}
kruskal.test(change ~ dose, data = data)                    # dose
wilcox.test(change ~ outdoors, data = data, exact = FALSE)  # outdoor exposure
```

Keeping all 150 islanders, neither factor is significant (dose p = 0.93,
outdoors p = 0.09). This agrees with the conclusion above.

## 2.6 Alternative model: ANCOVA

Instead of analysing the change score, ANCOVA models the after-time directly
and adjusts for each islander's baseline time. Age is also added because of
the small imbalance found in section 2.1.

```{r ancova}
ancova <- lm(after_5km ~ before_5km + Age + dose * outdoors, data = data)
anova(ancova)

ancova_wo <- lm(after_5km ~ before_5km + Age + dose * outdoors, data = data_wo)
anova(ancova_wo)
```

The ANCOVA leads to the same conclusion: no significant treatment effects,
with or without the outlier, and adjusting for age changes nothing.

## 2.7 Effect sizes

p-values say whether an effect is detectable; effect sizes say how large it is.

```{r effect_sizes}
partial_eta2 <- function(m) {
  tab <- summary(m)[[1]]
  ss  <- tab[, "Sum Sq"]
  round(ss[1:3] / (ss[1:3] + ss[4]), 4)
}
data.frame(term = c("Dose", "Outdoors", "Dose:Outdoors"),
           with_outlier = partial_eta2(model),
           without_outlier = partial_eta2(model_wo))
```

Every effect explains less than 2.5% of the variation in run-time change.

## 2.8 Power: could this design have detected the effect?

```{r power}
sd_resid <- sqrt(sum(residuals(model_wo)^2) / model_wo$df.residual)
power.t.test(n = 75, sd = sd_resid, power = 0.8, sig.level = 0.05)

# Observed outdoor difference (No minus Yes), without the outlier
diff(rev(tapply(data_wo$change, data_wo$outdoors, mean)))
```

With 75 islanders per outdoor group, the design had 80% power to detect a
difference of about **1.9 minutes**. The observed outdoor difference was only
about **1.1 minutes**, below that threshold. So "not significant" here does not
prove there is no effect; the experiment was too small to detect an effect of
this size reliably. Detecting a 1.1-minute difference with 80% power would
need about 240 islanders per group, roughly three times as many.

# Conclusions

1. Neither stimulant dose nor outdoor exposure had a statistically significant
   effect on 5 km run time, and there was no interaction.
2. The borderline outdoor effect in the original analysis (p = 0.066) depended
   on a single extreme observation; without it, p = 0.12.
3. The original model violated the normality assumption because of that
   observation. Checking residual diagnostics before trusting a p-value would
   have caught this.
4. Rank-based tests (which keep all data), an ANCOVA adjusted for baseline
   time and age, and effect sizes all point to the same conclusion.
5. The design could only detect effects of about 1.9 minutes or more. The
   observed outdoor effect (~1.1 minutes) is below that, so a larger
   experiment would be needed to settle the question.

# Limitations

- The data are simulated, so the results describe The Islands, not real people.
- The analysis uses a single pre/post measurement per islander; run times on
  any single day are noisy.
- Removing the outlier is a sensitivity check, not a correction. Without more
  information about that islander, there is no basis for excluding it from the
  main analysis.
